sysd-q-087.title: Heap
sysd-q-087.text: A heap keeps its most urgent item exactly where you can reach it: at the root. It is a tree in which each parent's key is at least (max heap) or at most (min heap) its children's keys. That is only partial order, not sorting, since siblings and cousins have no order between them. A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. Links are implied by indices: from index 0, node i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no extra memory is needed. Insertion adds an element at the end and sifts it up until the rule holds again. Removing the root moves the last element to the root and sifts it down. This makes a heap an efficient way to build a priority queue, and it also drives heapsort and graph algorithms such as {{ref:sysd-q-148}}.

sysd-q-088.title: Open banking
sysd-q-088.text: For years your bank's data stayed inside the bank. Open banking changes that: it lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through application programming interfaces (see {{ref:sysd-msg-001}}). With explicit customer consent, such a provider can read account information or initiate payments. Regulation drove the shift. The EU adopted PSD2 in October 2015, and in 2016 the UK required its nine biggest banks to give licensed startups transaction-level access. The openness has risks: hackers can target third-party apps, phishing can trick customers, and employees may hold excessive access privileges.

sysd-q-015.title: Designing a personal finance app
sysd-q-015.text:
Build the backend of a personal finance app in the style of Mint. A user connects a financial account, the service extracts its transactions and categorizes them, and the user analyzes monthly spending by category. Users may override a category by hand, but nothing is re-categorized automatically. The service also recommends a budget that the user can set manually, and it sends notifications when spending approaches or exceeds the budget. It must be highly available, and extra logging and analytics are out of scope.

The assumptions shape the design. Traffic is not evenly distributed, adding or removing accounts is rare, budget notifications need not be instant, and sellers determine a transaction's category. The automatic daily update covers only users active in the past 30 days. The scale is 10 million users with 30 million financial accounts and 50,000 sellers. They produce 5 billion transactions and 500 million read requests a month, a 10:1 write to read ratio. A transaction is about 50 bytes: user_id 8, created_at 5, seller 32 and amount 5. So 5 billion a month means 250 GB of new transaction content a month and 9 TB in 3 years. The average load is 2,000 transactions per second against 200 read requests per second. The system is write-heavy, because users make transactions daily but few visit the site daily.

To connect an account, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Accounts API server. That server writes the account to the SQL accounts table, indexed on id, user_id and created_at. The API is public REST. Extraction runs when the user first links an account, on manual refresh, and daily for users active in the past 30 days. It takes a while, so the API server queues a job on Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ. The Transaction Extraction Service pulls from the queue and stores raw transaction logs in an object store. It then calls the Category and Budget Services, and the Budget Service alerts users through a Notification Service. Finally it updates the SQL transactions and monthly_spending tables.

The Category Service seeds a seller-to-category dictionary with popular sellers: 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each take about 12 MB of memory. Sellers outside the seed are crowdsourced from user overrides, and a heap ({{ref:sysd-q-087}}) gives the top override in O(1). Budgets start from a generic template that allocates category amounts by income tier, so the 100 million budget items need not be stored. Only a user's overrides go in a budget_overrides table. Monthly spending can come from SQL queries over transactions into monthly_spending, which has far fewer rows than 5 billion transactions. Alternatively, MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files can categorize and aggregate, which reduces database load.

For reads, a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached holds sessions, category stats and recent transactions. The Read API server returns hits and otherwise reads the SQL database and updates the cache, the cache-aside pattern. Static content comes from a CDN-cached object store. The cache should serve the 200 average read requests per second, which are higher at peak, and it also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. SQL read replicas handle cache misses, unless they are bogged down replicating writes. Writes are the harder side, since 2,000 average writes per second might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. The remedies are federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and perhaps moving some data to NoSQL. Keep only a month of transactions in the database. The rest goes to a data warehouse or object store, which comfortably handles 250 GB of new content a month.

Remember the shape of the load. The system is write-heavy, extraction is slow so a queue carries it, and the few reads are served from a cache.

sysd-q-068.title: Doubly linked list
sysd-q-068.text: A doubly linked list lets you walk in either direction. It is a chain of nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node. The head and tail are directly accessible, and any node can start a new traversal. Adding or removing a node changes more links than in a singly linked list. It is still simpler and often more efficient, since a node already links to its predecessor and no traversal is needed to find it. Removing the first or last node needs care so the head and tail references are updated.

sysd-q-001.title: Designing a search query cache
sysd-q-001.text:
Build a cache that remembers the results of recent search queries. The service handles a user's search request that hits the cache and one that misses it, and it must be highly available. The assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, and popular queries should almost always be in the cache. Serving from cache needs fast lookups, and latency between machines must be low. Memory is limited yet millions of queries must be cached, so the design must decide what to keep or remove and how to expire or refresh entries.

The scale is 10 million users, 10 billion queries per month and 4,000 requests per second. A cache entry holds a 50-byte query, a 20-byte title and a 200-byte snippet, 270 bytes in total. Suppose all 10 billion queries were unique and all were stored. The data would be 2.7 TB per month: 270 bytes per search times 10 billion searches. That is why the cache cannot keep everything. A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached serves popular queries, cutting read latency and sparing the Reverse Index and Document Services. Reading 1 MB sequentially takes about 250 microseconds from memory, while SSD takes 4x and disk 80x longer.

The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization, converts it to boolean operations and checks the cache. On a hit, the memory cache moves the entry to the front of the list and returns the cached contents. On a miss, the Query API gets ranked matching documents from the Reverse Index Service. It gets titles and snippets from the Document Service, then caches the entry at the front of the list.

Since cache capacity is limited, a least recently used (LRU) approach expires the older entries. The cache is a doubly linked list plus a hash table. New items are added at the head, items to expire are removed from the tail, and the hash table gives fast lookup of each list node. The list itself is the subject of {{ref:sysd-q-068}}. Entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or page rank changes. The simplest way is a maximum time an entry may stay cached, the time to live (TTL), and this approach is cache-aside.

To handle the request load and the memory needed, scale the cache horizontally. Giving each machine its own cache is simple but likely gives a low hit rate, and giving each a full copy is simple but wastes memory. Sharding the cache across all machines in the cluster is more complex but likely the best option. A hash such as machine = hash(query) picks the machine, and consistent hashing is likely wanted. The thing to remember is the pairing: a doubly linked list plus a hash table gives fast lookup and cheap eviction. A hash of the query then spreads the cache over many machines.

sysd-q-019.title: Designing a sales rank by category
sysd-q-019.text:
Build a service that calculates the past week's most popular products by category and lets users view them, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope. The assumptions: traffic is uneven, an item can be in multiple categories but cannot change category, and there are no subcategories. Results must be updated hourly, though more popular products might need more frequent updates.

The scale is 10 million products, 1 billion transactions per month and 100 billion read requests per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio. A transaction is about 40 bytes: created_at 5, product_id 8, category_id 4, seller_id 8, buyer_id 8, quantity 4 and total_price 5 bytes. That is 40 GB of new transaction content per month, which is 40 bytes times 1 billion transactions. Over 3 years it is 1.44 TB, assuming most are new transactions rather than updates. The average load is 400 transactions per second and 40,000 read requests per second.

Raw Sales API server log files go to a managed object store such as Amazon S3, rather than a self-managed distributed file system. The Sales Rank Service runs MapReduce with those logs as input and writes the results to an aggregate table, sales_rank, in a SQL database. The MapReduce has several steps. First it transforms records to (category, product_id) with sum(quantity), then it performs a distributed sort. The sorted list is inserted into the sales_rank table. That table is indexed on id, category_id and product_id, for log-time lookups instead of scanning the whole table and to keep the data in memory.

To view rankings, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Read API server, which reads the SQL sales_rank table. The public API is REST, with RPC for internal calls. The 40,000 average read requests per second, higher at peak, should be handled by a memory cache instead of the database, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. With such a large volume of reads, SQL read replicas might not handle the cache misses, so additional SQL scaling patterns are probably needed.

The 400 average writes per second, higher at peak, might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. SQL scaling patterns include federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and some data might also move to NoSQL. The analytics database could be a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery. Keep a limited time period in the database and the rest in a warehouse or an object store, which handles 40 GB of new content per month. The thing to remember is the split: the rank is computed in batch by MapReduce from raw logs, and the heavy read traffic is answered from a cache.

sysd-q-155.title: Social graph
sysd-q-155.text: A social network is a graph before it is anything else. A social graph represents social relations between entities, and it is a model of a social network. Relations can be mutual or one-way. On Twitter the relation between users is unidirectional, unlike classical networks such as Facebook, which makes information propagation closer to how information spreads in real life. In 2012, Twitter's social graph held 537 million accounts connected by 23.95 billion links. Such graphs are typically stored in graph databases, and Facebook uses TAO, a custom distributed system optimized for fast reads at massive scale.

sysd-q-159.title: Adjacency matrix
sysd-q-159.text: A graph can be stored as a table of ones and zeros. An adjacency matrix is a square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent. For a simple graph of n vertices it is an n-by-n matrix. Its element Aij is 1 if an edge runs from vertex i to vertex j, else 0, and its diagonal is 0 because simple graphs have no loops. An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix, a directed graph's matrix can be asymmetric, and edge weights can be stored directly in the elements. The matrix tests in constant time whether two vertices are adjacent, but listing a vertex's neighbors means scanning a whole row, which takes O(|V|) time. Each entry needs one bit, so a directed graph fits in |V|²/8 bytes. For a large sparse graph, {{ref:sysd-q-158}} need less storage.

sysd-q-158.title: Adjacency list
sysd-q-158.text: What does this vertex connect to? An adjacency list answers by storing, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbors. Implementations vary. One is a hash table from each vertex to an array of neighbors, and another is an array indexed by vertex number pointing to linked lists. A third uses vertex and edge objects, which use more memory but can store data per edge. Listing a vertex's neighbors takes constant time per neighbor, so the total time is proportional to the vertex's degree. Testing whether an edge exists is slower. With unsorted neighbors it takes time proportional to the smaller degree of the two vertices. With a sorted array and binary search it is logarithmic in the degree. For a sparse graph the list is far more space-efficient than {{ref:sysd-q-159}}. Its space is proportional to the vertices plus edges, against the square of the vertices for a matrix.

sysd-q-153.title: Breadth-first search
sysd-q-153.text: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level. It starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level. It keeps a queue of nodes met but not yet explored, labels each vertex explored when it is enqueued, and stores a parent link on each vertex. The parent links trace the shortest path back to the root. BFS uses a first-in-first-out queue where depth-first search uses a last-in-first-out stack. It finds the path with the fewest edges between two nodes, an advantage over depth-first search. It is also complete: it reaches a goal if one exists, even in an infinite graph. Time is O(|V|+|E|), since every vertex and edge is explored in the worst case. On an unweighted graph, BFS is {{ref:sysd-q-148}} with the priority queue degenerated into a plain queue.

sysd-q-154.title: Shortest path problem
sysd-q-154.text: A road map is a graph. Intersections are vertices, road segments are edges weighted by length, travel time or cost, and directed edges model one-way streets. The shortest path problem asks for a path between two vertices so that the sum of its edge weights is as small as possible. The right algorithm depends on the graph. For a single source with non-negative weights the choice is {{ref:sysd-q-148}}. Bellman–Ford suits weights that may be negative, {{ref:sysd-q-149}} handles a single pair using heuristics, and Floyd–Warshall handles all pairs. On an unweighted graph, {{ref:sysd-q-153}} solves the single-source problem in O(E + V). Adding a constraint, such as keeping a second metric under a threshold, makes the problem NP-complete. Real roads are harder still: travel time varies with traffic, road work, weather and accidents, and there is no accepted definition of an optimal path under uncertainty.

sysd-q-157.title: Bidirectional search
sysd-q-157.text: Two searches that start at opposite ends and meet in the middle can beat one search that goes all the way. Bidirectional search finds a shortest path by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet. With branching factor b and start-to-goal distance d, each of the two searches costs O(b^(d/2)), and their sum is much less than the O(b^d) of a single search. The backward search must be able to find, for any node, the parent nodes that have an edge into it. Termination needs care: Goldberg and others explained the correct conditions for bidirectional Dijkstra, and bidirectional A* needs a special stopping criterion. On single-pair queries, bidirectional Dijkstra often visits far fewer vertices than the one-directional version. Each search explores roughly half the space. {{ref:sysd-q-150}} also answer queries with a bidirectional search.

sysd-q-156.title: Six degrees of separation
sysd-q-156.text: Any two people are supposedly six or fewer friend-of-a-friend links apart. The idea generalizes to an average social distance that is logarithmic in population size. With 30 contacts each, six rounds of handshakes would reach a population as large as the United States. Measurements come close: in a 2007 study the average among 240 million Microsoft Messenger users was 6, and on Twitter in 2010 it was 4.67. Detractors argue that Milgram's small-world experiment did not demonstrate the claim, and they call it an academic urban myth.

sysd-q-064.title: Designing a social network graph
sysd-q-064.text:
Build a service where a user searches for another person and sees the shortest path to that person. It must be highly available. The assumptions: traffic is uneven, some searches are more popular than others, the graph data will not fit on a single machine, and graph edges are unweighted. The scale is 100 million users with 50 friends each on average, giving 5 billion friend relationships. There are 1 billion friend searches per month, or 400 search requests per second.

The exercise avoids graph-specific solutions such as GraphQL or a graph database like Neo4j. Without that constraint, a graph database or graph query language could be used. Without millions of users (vertices) and billions of friend relationships (edges), a general breadth-first search (BFS) would solve this unweighted shortest path task. At this size users cannot all fit on one machine, so they are sharded across Person Servers, which are accessed through a Lookup Service.

The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Search API server, which forwards to the User Graph Service. The User Graph Service asks the Lookup Service for the Person Server holding the current user and retrieves that user's friend_ids. It then runs a BFS with the user as source and the friend_ids as adjacent nodes. For each adjacent node it must again ask the Lookup Service which Person Server stores that id, a step with potential for optimization. The public API is REST, and internal communication could use remote procedure calls.

Person data can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached. That cuts response times and downstream traffic at 400 average read requests per second, higher at peak, especially for repeated searches and well-connected people. Complete or partial BFS traversals can be stored in the cache to speed later lookups, or computed offline in batch and stored in a NoSQL database. To reduce machine jumps, batch friend lookups hosted on the same Person Server, and shard Person Servers by location, since friends generally live closer to each other.

Two more ideas shrink the search. Run two BFS searches at once, one from the source and one from the destination, then merge the two paths, which is the method of {{ref:sysd-q-157}}. Start the BFS from people with many friends, since they more likely shorten the degrees of separation to the target. Set a time or hop limit before asking the user whether to keep searching. The thing to remember is that the sharded graph makes every hop a possible machine jump. Batching, location sharding and a two-way search all aim to cut the cost of each search.

sysd-q-066.title: Scaling a website in stages
sysd-q-066.text: A website that starts on one server cannot stay there once the traffic arrives. This is how a simplified e-commerce site grows, from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture. It has an inventory service for product descriptions and inventory, and a user service for registration, login and user information. As the user base grows, one application server cannot handle the traffic, so the application server and the database server move onto two separate servers. When one application server is still not enough, a cluster is deployed, and a load balancer routes incoming requests so each server gets an even load. If the database becomes the bottleneck, frequent read queries go to read replicas by separating reads from writes, which greatly increases database write throughput. When one database cannot carry both the inventory and user tables, there are three options. One is adding CPU and RAM, which has a hard limit. Another is partitioning horizontally across more database servers, and the third is adding a caching layer to offload reads. Finally the functions are modularized into separate services.

sysd-q-160.title: Virtual private cloud
sysd-q-160.text: A virtual private cloud gives one organization a private corner of a public cloud. It is an on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources that isolates that organization's resources from the others. Isolation normally comes from a private IP subnet and a virtual communication construct per user, such as a VLAN or a set of encrypted channels. A per-VPC virtual private network function secures remote access through authentication and encryption. Amazon's VPC lets EC2 instances be connected to legacy infrastructure over an IPsec VPN. On Google Cloud a VPC is a global resource and its subnets are regional.

sysd-q-065.title: Scaling a system to millions of users
sysd-q-065.text:
Scale a service from a few users to millions on AWS, discussing general scaling patterns, since the principles apply outside AWS too. A user makes a read or write request, and the service processes it, stores user data and returns results. It must keep high availability as it grows. Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. The assumptions are uneven traffic and a need for relational data. The target is 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio, at 1 KB per write. That is an estimated 1 TB of new content per month and 36 TB in 3 years. The average load is 400 writes per second and 40,000 reads per second.

With one or two users, start with a single box for simplicity: a web server on EC2, storage for user data and a MySQL database. Start with SQL because relational data is needed. Scale vertically when needed, and monitor to find bottlenecks. Vertical scaling, a bigger box, can get very expensive and leaves no redundancy or failover, and the alternative is horizontal scaling. An Elastic IP gives a public endpoint that survives reboots and eases failover, and DNS such as Route 53 maps the domain to it. Open only the needed ports: 80, 443 and 22 for SSH from whitelisted IPs.

As users grow, vertical scaling gets expensive and blocks scaling MySQL and the web server independently. So store static content in a managed object store such as S3, and move MySQL to a separate box, for example RDS. The split adds complexity, changes to the web server and new security needs. Secure it with encryption in transit and at rest. Put the web server in a public subnet and everything else in a private subnet, all inside a virtual private cloud ({{ref:sysd-q-160}}).

When one web server bottlenecks at peak hours, scale horizontally behind a load balancer such as ELB or HAProxy, terminating SSL there. Use multiple web servers and MySQL in master-slave failover across multiple availability zones. Then separate the web servers, running as reverse proxy, from the application servers and scale each independently, for example read-API and write-API servers. Move static and some dynamic content to a CDN such as CloudFront.

For a read-heavy 100:1 workload, move frequently accessed content and session data to a memory cache such as ElastiCache, which makes the web servers stateless. Add MySQL read replicas too, splitting reads and writes in the web server. Traffic spikes in business hours and drops afterward. Autoscaling groups for each web and application server type, across availability zones, keep up with the spikes and cut costs.

Near the full constraints, keep a limited period of data in MySQL and the rest in a warehouse such as Redshift. Scale the memory cache for 40,000 reads per second, though read replicas may struggle with cache misses. The 400 writes per second may strain a single SQL write master-slave. Use federation, denormalization or SQL tuning, and consider moving suitable data to NoSQL such as DynamoDB. Work that need not be real-time goes to queues and workers. In a photo service, the application server queues a job, and a worker creates the thumbnail, updates the database and stores the thumbnail in the object store. The thing to remember is the loop: each fix removes one bottleneck and exposes the next, so benchmark, profile and fix again.

openers.design-a-personal-finance-app-like-mint: A personal finance app has four jobs: connect a financial account, extract its transactions, categorize them, and analyze monthly spending by category. Users can override a category by hand, but nothing is re-categorized automatically. Two building blocks come first in this chapter. A heap is a tree in which the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root, and open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through APIs. Then the worked design builds the whole service.
openers.design-a-cache-for-the-most-recent-searc: What happens when a search request finds its answer already in the cache, and what happens when it does not? The service in this chapter must handle both, and it must stay highly available. The chapter first introduces a data structure, the doubly linked list, whose nodes each hold a data field plus links to the previous and the next node. Then it puts that structure to work in the design of a cache for recent search queries.
openers.design-a-sales-rank-by-category: Which products sold best this past week, in each category? This service calculates the answer and lets users view it, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope. The chapter is a single worked design.
openers.design-the-data-structures-for-a-social: A social network is a graph, and the interview question is how to search it. A social graph represents social relations between entities, and it can be stored as an adjacency matrix, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent, or as an adjacency list that stores an unordered list of neighbors for each vertex. Breadth-first search explores it level by level, the shortest path problem asks for the path with the smallest total edge weight, and bidirectional search runs one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal. The folk idea of six degrees of separation says a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people. The worked design lets a user search for someone and see the shortest path to that person.
openers.scale-a-system-to-millions-of-users-on-a: A website that starts on one server has to grow without falling over. This chapter follows a simplified e-commerce site as it evolves from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture. Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. The chapter also introduces the virtual private cloud, an on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others. AWS-specific details are not required, since the principles apply outside AWS too.

reviews.design-a-personal-finance-app-like-mint: Open banking explains where the transactions come from: banks expose APIs that authorized third parties may use, with the customer's consent. The heap turns up inside the Category Service, where it gives the top seller override in O(1). The worked design then surrounds these pieces with a queue for slow extraction, a cache for the few reads, and SQL and object storage for the data. The sizing starts from one number, 5 billion transactions a month.
reviews.design-a-cache-for-the-most-recent-searc: The doubly linked list is what makes eviction cheap: a node already links to its predecessor, so removing it needs no traversal. The worked design pairs the list with a hash table, so lookups are fast and the least recently used entries sit at the tail. A time to live keeps entries fresh, and sharding by a hash of the query, ideally with consistent hashing, spreads the cache over many machines.
reviews.design-a-sales-rank-by-category: The sales rank is a batch job with a read-heavy front. Raw Sales API logs go to an object store, a multi-step MapReduce turns them into (category, product_id) sums, and the sorted result lands in an indexed sales_rank table. Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, so a memory cache answers most views while SQL scaling patterns cover the 400 writes per second. Older data moves to a warehouse or an object store.
reviews.design-the-data-structures-for-a-social: The chapter moves from model to method to design. The social graph is the model, and the adjacency matrix and adjacency list are two ways to store it: the matrix tests adjacency in constant time, while the list lists neighbors cheaply and saves space on sparse graphs. Breadth-first search finds the path with the fewest edges, the shortest path problem says when other algorithms are needed, and bidirectional search runs two searches that meet. Six degrees of separation adds the expectation that paths are short, with measured averages of 6 on Messenger and 4.67 on Twitter. The worked design shards 100 million users across Person Servers and runs the search from both ends.
reviews.scale-a-system-to-millions-of-users-on-a: The chapter tells the same story twice. The staged account moves from one server to separate servers, a load-balanced cluster, read replicas, and then partitioned databases, a cache and separate services. The worked example repeats the loop with numbers, 10 million users and 40,000 reads per second at a 100:1 read to write ratio, and names AWS pieces for each step. A virtual private cloud keeps those pieces private, with a public subnet for the web server and a private subnet for the rest.
